contentHtml:
Prem Ranjan, Director and Audiologist, MED-EL India, in an interview with Kalyani Sharma, discusses the gaps in India’s hearing healthcare ecosystem, advances in hearing implant technology, barriers to early diagnosis and intervention, and the need to improve affordability and access to hearing care beyond metro cities

What are the key gaps in India’s hearing healthcare ecosystem, particularly in early diagnosis and intervention?

If I had to name a single gap, I would say it is the time between what we already know about early hearing loss and what actually happens to a family during the first year of a baby’s life. Newborn screening is not yet done consistently everywhere, and because awareness is still low, a child who hasn’t started speaking is commonly advised to wait and see, on the reasonable-sounding grounds that some children are late talkers. That wait can quietly cost a year or two or even more. Meanwhile, audiologists, diagnostic facilities and rehabilitation services are thin on the ground in many places, and families in underserved communities feel it most. So my first ask is simple: make early screening a priority and routine at every maternity hospital/ care facility, and make sure a result that needs follow-up actually leads to proper intervention and care. A test at birth costs very little compared with what a missed diagnosis costs a child later, in school and in life.

How have hearing implants evolved beyond conventional hearing aids, and which patients can benefit from them?

Hearing implants go beyond conventional hearing aids by addressing different types and degrees of hearing loss. While hearing aids amplify sound, cochlear implants bypass damaged parts of the inner ear and electrically stimulate the hearing nerve. They may benefit children and adults with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss who receive limited benefit from hearing aids, following specialist assessment. Other implantable solutions including bone conduction, and middle ear implants, can help people with specific conductive and or mixed hearing losses of different degrees.

Advances in technology are also making audio processors smaller, lighter and more sophisticated. MED-EL’s Sonnet3, the smallest and lightest behind-the-ear processor we’ve made, was launched in India at CIGICON 2026 in Agra.

What are the major barriers to timely diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation for people with hearing loss in India?

Much of the delay starts at home, and nobody is really to blame for it. A toddler who doesn’t react to a loud clatter in the kitchen, or who still has no words by the age of two, will often be met with kind reassurance from relatives that he is shy or that she will speak in her own time. This can mean valuable months pass before the child’s hearing is assessed. The relation of hearing to speech language is often overlooked.

Once a family does decide to act, the next obstacle is distance and accessibility to professional care, because most audiologists, speech therapists and implant surgeons work in the large cities, so parents from a small town may find themselves travelling hundreds of kilometres for every appointment and giving up a day’s income each time.

Cost matters, of course, but the device is only one piece. The journey also includes assessment, surgery, programming, long term auditory rehabilitation and regular follow-ups. Insurance and public schemes may not cover every stage. Sustained rehabilitation is particularly important; without consistent therapy and follow-ups patients may not achieve the full potential benefit from the hearing technology.

How are advances in electrode design, hearing preservation and robotic insertion shaping hearing implant outcomes?

The last few millimetres of the electrode insertion matter a great deal. The cochlea is a delicate structure, and if it is damaged while the electrode goes in, whatever natural hearing the person had left can be lost. That’s the thinking behind electrode arrays that are straight, softer and flexible, so they slide in with less force. Our FLEX arrays follow that thinking, and they carry FDA approval for hearing preservation, which in plain terms means they are designed so that it becomes likely that a person can keep whatever functional hearing remains after surgery and for a long term. An adult who still hears the low pitches naturally can then benefit from electric acoustic stimulation, with the natural ear covering the low frequencies and the implant covering the mid to high ones. There is growing interest in robotic-assisted insertion as well, because a machine can advance the electrode at a slow, steady and repeatable speed, with the surgeon’s judgement at the centre of the procedure. What we are all working towards, in the end, is clearer speech, better music enjoyment and a sound that feels closer to natural to the person hearing it.

What can be done to make advanced hearing implants more affordable and accessible, particularly beyond metro cities?

I would keep affordability and accessibility apart in this discussion, since solving one doesn’t automatically solve the other. On the cost side, a number of public hospitals already provide implants under government programmes and tenders, which is a model worth strengthening and extending to Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, and insurers, for their part, should move towards covering the whole journey, from surgery and rehabilitation to aftercare and long-term maintenance, rather than reimbursing only the device.

Another aspect is covering implant procedure for only one ear versus both the ears which will bring natural advantages of binaural hearing. Access is a separate challenge, and telemedicine can help here by handling counselling, follow-up and some remote checks, which spares families from making so many long journeys, although it cannot replace in-person care for the assessments and procedures that have to be done in-person. For that reason we need trained audiologists, therapists and surgeons closer to where patients live, with industry helping through training and clinical support, so that a family in a smaller town is connected to a specialist centre and a handful of metro hospitals aren’t left carrying the whole load.

How has India’s hearing implant market evolved, and what should be the priorities for expanding access over the next five years?

The market has come a long way. MED-EL has had its own subsidiary in India since 2006, and in the years since, implant centres have multiplied, surgical teams have grown and public schemes have put implants within reach of families who couldn’t have afforded them. Newer technology also reaches India faster now. SONNET 3 has already reached Indian users this year, and TICI UNICO, the world’s first totally implantable cochlear implant, was launched in Europe in September 2026, although its availability in India will depend on regulatory approvals. Looking at the next five years, what I would like to see is newborn screening carried out consistently with proper follow-up for every newborn or at least a must for high-risk births, rehabilitation services strong enough to support the years of therapy on which outcomes depend, and access that reaches beyond the metros through connected care networks. Financing must also support the entire care pathway, from diagnosis and implantation to long-term rehabilitation. Ultimately progress should be measured not just by technological advances, but by how many people can access them and benefit from them.
